**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:** The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Never issue multiple `office_read` calls in parallel (in the same turn). One call, wait for the result, then the next. Parallel calls WILL crash the resident.

# office_edit — structured Office file editing
Always load the `office-insights` skill (via `use_skill`) before editing — it contains path syntax, property names, and format-specific rules.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:**
The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Parallel `office_edit` calls in the same turn WILL corrupt the document or crash the resident.
**Use `operation:batch` when adding multiple elements (e.g. a full slide with shapes).** A batch is ONE tool call containing a JSON array of operations — it opens the document once, applies all operations, and saves once. This is faster and avoids the parallelism trap entirely.
Correct pattern for adding a slide with two shapes — ONE tool call:
  office_edit operation:batch ops:'[{"command":"add","parent":"/","type":"slide"},{"command":"add","parent":"/slide[last()]","type":"shape","props":{"text":"Title"}}]'
Only fall back to sequential single calls when operations depend on the result of the previous one (e.g. reading back a path before using it).

Do NOT pass comma-separated patterns (e.g. "**/*.ts,**/*.tsx") — use a single pattern per call instead (e.g. "**/*.{ts,tsx}" or two separate calls).

---
name: docs-drift-check
description: Audit a repository's documentation (README, CONTRIBUTING, docs folder) against the actual code and list every statement that is no longer true, with file-and-line evidence. Writes DRIFT_REPORT.md and DRIFT_REPORT.json. Use when asked to check, audit or verify docs for drift or outdated content.
---

# DocDrift: documentation drift audit

Goal: find every place where the documentation says something the code no longer supports,
prove it with evidence, and write one clear report for humans (Markdown) and one for tools
(JSON, used by the DocDrift dashboard).

Keep costs low. Do not re-read files you have already read. Use read-only `explore`
subagents for checking (they run on a lighter model and cannot change files).

<Steps>
<Step>
**Find the target.** The target folder is the folder the user names (for example
`audits/flask-realworld-example-app`). If none is named, the target is the workspace root.
All paths in the report are written relative to the target folder.
Never audit the DocDrift tool's own files (`.bob/`, `dashboard/`, `benchmark/`, `bob_sessions/`)
unless the target folder is the workspace root and the user asked for it.
</Step>

<Step>
**Find the docs.** If the user named doc files, audit only those. Otherwise audit, in order:
README (any of README.md, README.rst, README.txt, README), CONTRIBUTING, other top-level
.md/.rst files, then a docs/ folder if it is small (at most 10 files; otherwise only the
README and CONTRIBUTING, and say so in the report). Skip CHANGELOG, LICENSE, auto-generated
API reference and anything in node_modules, vendor, venv, .venv, bin, obj, dist, build, .git.
</Step>

<Step>
**Record the licence.** Read the LICENSE file (or the "license" field of package.json,
pyproject.toml or setup.cfg) and record the licence name, for example MIT or Apache-2.0.
If none is found, record "NOT FOUND". This matters because only permissively licensed
projects may be used in the hackathon.
</Step>

<Step>
**Extract claims.** Read the docs and pull out every statement that can be checked
against the code. Sort each one into a category from `categories.md`:
COMMAND, PATH, ENV, API, VERSION, DEPENDENCY, COUNT.
Give each claim an ID (C1, C2, ...) and record the doc file and line it came from.
Ignore opinions, marketing text and things that cannot be checked from the repo.
Write the claim list into your todo list so progress is visible.
</Step>

<Step>
**Check claims in parallel.** Spawn one read-only `explore` subagent per category
that has claims (up to six). Give each subagent:
- the target folder,
- the list of claims in its category (ID, exact quoted text, doc location), and
- the checking rules for that category from `categories.md`.

Each subagent must return, for every claim, one verdict:
- OK: the code confirms it (cite file:line),
- DRIFT: the code contradicts it (cite file:line and say what the truth is),
- UNVERIFIED: no clear evidence either way (say what was searched).

If there are fewer than 5 claims in total, check them directly instead of spawning subagents.
Also run the ENV reverse check from `categories.md` (settings the code reads that the docs
never mention), even if there are no ENV claims.
</Step>

<Step>
**Double-check every DRIFT.** Before reporting a DRIFT:
1. Re-open the cited code evidence yourself and confirm it. If it is weak, downgrade the
   claim to UNVERIFIED. A false alarm is worse than a missed problem.
2. Re-open the doc file and confirm the quoted text is on exactly the cited line number.
   Line numbers start at 1. If the quote is on a different line, correct the number.
</Step>

<Step>
**Group by root cause.** If several DRIFT claims come from the same underlying problem
(for example a missing file that is mentioned in two places), report them as ONE finding
and list all the affected claim IDs and doc lines in it. Each claim still counts
separately in the trust score.
</Step>

<Step>
**Rate severity** for each finding using `categories.md`:
HIGH (a new developer following the docs will fail), MEDIUM (confusing or misleading),
LOW (cosmetic or minor).
</Step>

<Step>
**Write the reports** into the target folder:
1. `DRIFT_REPORT.md`, using exactly the layout in `report-template.md`.
2. `DRIFT_REPORT.json`, using exactly the structure in `report-schema.md`.
   For `audited_at`, use today's date from your environment details (YYYY-MM-DD). Never guess a
   date; if you do not know it, write null. It must be valid
   JSON (double quotes, no comments, no trailing commas) and contain the same numbers and
   findings as the Markdown report.

Trust score = OK claims / (OK + DRIFT claims) x 100, rounded to a whole number.
UNVERIFIED claims are listed but not counted in the score. If there are no OK or DRIFT
claims at all, the score is null.
</Step>

<Step>
**Finish** with a short chat summary: target, licence, number of claims checked, DRIFT
findings by severity, and the trust score. If you were started as a subtask, return this
summary as your result so the Pilot can use it.
</Step>
</Steps>

1 | # Claim categories and how to check them
2 | 
3 | ## COMMAND
4 | Shell commands the docs tell people to run (install, build, test, start, migrate).
5 | Check:
6 | - npm / yarn / pnpm scripts exist in package.json "scripts".
7 | - make targets exist in the Makefile.
8 | - dotnet commands point to real .csproj / .sln files and projects.
9 | - python commands point to real modules or scripts; pip install uses real requirement files.
10 | - docker / docker compose commands point to real Dockerfiles, compose files and service names.
11 | - Flags and arguments are still accepted by the script, if the script is in the repo.
12 | 
13 | ## PATH
14 | Files and folders the docs mention (config files, entry points, folders to edit).
15 | Check: the path exists exactly as written (case matters). If not, search for a file
16 | with the same name elsewhere. If one is found, it was probably moved: report the new path.
17 | A PATH claim only needs the file or folder to exist. If a file is listed by a directory
18 | listing or glob but its contents are blocked (for example by .bobignore), it still
19 | exists: mark the claim OK, not UNVERIFIED.
20 | 
21 | ## COUNT
22 | Numbers the docs state about the code ("68 tests", "5 endpoints", "3 models").
23 | Check: count carefully, and watch for things that multiply the count.
24 | For tests in particular, @pytest.mark.parametrize, test classes, and fixtures with
25 | params make the real number of tests larger than the number of `def test_` lines.
26 | If any of these are present and you cannot run the test collector, mark the claim
27 | UNVERIFIED and explain why, instead of reporting DRIFT from a simple text count.
28 | 
29 | ## ENV
30 | Environment variables and config keys (DATABASE_URL, PORT, API keys, appsettings keys).
31 | Check:
32 | - Search the code for where the variable is read (process.env, os.environ, os.getenv,
33 |   Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable, IConfiguration keys, .env.example).
34 | - DRIFT if the docs name a variable the code never reads, or if the code requires a
35 |   variable the docs setup section never mentions (report the missing one too).
36 | - Also check default values and ports if the docs state them.
37 | - ALWAYS do a reverse check, even if the docs make no ENV claims: search the code for
38 |   every environment variable and config key it reads, and list any that the docs never
39 |   mention. Record each one's name, where it is read (file:line), and its default value
40 |   if the code has one. Never read or quote the values in .env files: only the names.
41 |   This list is what the fixer needs to write correct setup instructions.
42 | - Report the undocumented settings as a DRIFT finding (not just a note) when either:
43 |   (a) a doc file, including comments in .env.example, promises that the settings are
44 |       documented ("a complete list is in the documentation") and they are not, or
45 |   (b) the code REQUIRES a setting (no default, startup fails without it) and the setup
46 |       instructions never mention it.
47 |   Otherwise list them only in the "Undocumented settings" table.
48 | 
49 | ## API
50 | Code examples, function / class names, parameters, HTTP routes and methods.
51 | Check:
52 | - Functions and classes in examples exist with the same name and parameter list.
53 | - HTTP routes exist with the same path and method (look at route decorators,
54 |   controllers, router definitions, MapGet/MapPost calls).
55 | - Request/response field names match the models.
56 | 
57 | ## VERSION
58 | Runtime and tool versions (Node 18, Python 3.11, .NET 8, Java 17).
59 | Check against: package.json "engines", .nvmrc, .python-version, pyproject.toml,
60 | global.json, TargetFramework in .csproj, Dockerfile base images, CI config files.
61 | 
62 | ## DEPENDENCY
63 | Libraries and services the docs say are needed (PostgreSQL, Redis, a specific package).
64 | Check: they appear in dependency files, docker-compose services or config.
65 | DRIFT if the docs require something the project no longer uses, or the project
66 | clearly needs something the docs never mention.
67 | 
68 | # Evidence must come from the repository
69 | 
70 | A DRIFT verdict needs evidence inside the repository (a file and line that contradicts
71 | the docs). Knowledge about the outside world (a tool release, a deprecated command, a newer
72 | library version) is NOT evidence of drift, because the docs may still match the code.
73 | List such observations separately under "Outdated practices" (advice only, never counted in
74 | the trust score, never fixed automatically), and say plainly that they come from general
75 | knowledge, not from the code.
76 | 
77 | # Severity guide
78 | 
79 | - HIGH: following the docs will fail. Examples: a setup command that does not exist,
80 |   a required env var that is missing from the docs, a wrong runtime major version.
81 | - MEDIUM: misleading or will waste time but does not block. Examples: a moved file,
82 |   an outdated code example, a renamed route in an API table.
83 | - LOW: cosmetic. Examples: a stale default value that is rarely used, wrong casing
84 |   in a path on a case-insensitive system, outdated optional steps.

1 | # Time Series Forecasting: LSTM vs Prophet vs ARIMA
2 | 
3 | Trains and compares three forecasting models on any stock ticker, serves predictions through a
4 | REST API, and presents everything in an interactive dashboard.
5 | 
6 | Pick a ticker and a date range, train all three models on it, then compare how they actually
7 | performed on data none of them saw during training.
8 | 
9 | ---
10 | 
11 | ## What it does
12 | 
13 | - **Fetches live data** from Yahoo Finance for any ticker, over any date range up to 5 years
14 | - **Trains three models** on the same data: a PyTorch LSTM, Facebook Prophet, and ARIMA
15 | - **Backtests them** against a held-out test period and records the results
16 | - **Serves forecasts** through a FastAPI REST API, including an ensemble that averages all three
17 | - **Versions every training run**, so retraining on 2 years vs 5 years of data produces two
18 |   separately comparable models rather than one overwriting the other
19 | 
20 | ---
21 | 
22 | ## Quick start
23 | 
24 | ### Option A: Docker (recommended)
25 | 
26 | Runs the API, dashboard, and a PostgreSQL database together, with no local Python setup at all.
27 | 
28 | ```bash
29 | docker compose up --build
30 | ```
31 | 
32 | Then open:
33 | - Dashboard: http://localhost:8501
34 | - API docs: http://localhost:8000/docs
35 | 
36 | The first build takes several minutes - PyTorch and Prophet are large. Later starts are fast.
37 | 
38 | ### Option B: Running locally
39 | 
40 | ```bash
41 | python -m venv venv
42 | venv\Scripts\activate        # Windows
43 | # source venv/bin/activate   # macOS / Linux
44 | 
45 | pip install -r requirements.txt
46 | 
47 | copy .env.example .env       # Windows
48 | # cp .env.example .env       # macOS / Linux
49 | ```
50 | 
51 | The default `.env` uses SQLite, so no database server is needed. To use PostgreSQL instead, set
52 | `DB_CONNECTION_STRING` in `.env`. Then, in two terminals:
53 | 
54 | ```bash
55 | uvicorn src.api.server:app --reload    # terminal 1
56 | streamlit run dashboard/main.py         # terminal 2
57 | ```
58 | 
59 | ---
60 | 
61 | ## Using it
62 | 
63 | 1. Open the dashboard and enter a ticker (e.g. `AAPL`)
64 | 2. Click **Train** in the sidebar - this trains all three models and takes a minute or two
65 | 3. Once training finishes, the **Forecasts** and **Comparison** tabs become available
66 | 
67 | The Forecasts tab plots the prediction against what actually happened. This works because
68 | forecasts begin at the model's training cutoff rather than today, so real prices usually already
69 | exist for part of the forecast window - making it a real accuracy check, not just a projection.
70 | 
71 | Nothing is pre-trained: a ticker must be trained before it can be forecast. `GET /tickers` lists
72 | which ones are ready.
73 | 
74 | ---
75 | 
76 | ## API endpoints
77 | 
78 | | Method | Endpoint | Purpose |
79 | |---|---|---|
80 | | POST | `/health` | API status, database connectivity, trained tickers |
81 | | GET | `/models` | Which tickers have a trained model ready |
82 | | GET | `/historical?ticker=AAPL&days=365` | Real price history |
83 | | POST | `/retrain` | Start training a ticker (returns immediately with a job id) |
84 | | GET | `/retrain-status/{job_id}` | Check on a training job |
85 | | POST | `/predict` | Get predictions (`lstm`, `prophet`, `arima`, or `ensemble`) |
86 | | GET | `/model-comparison?ticker=AAPL` | Each model's accuracy from its last training run |
87 | 
88 | Interactive docs at http://localhost:8000/docs once the API is running.
89 | 
90 | **Training is asynchronous.** `POST /retrain` returns a `job_id` right away rather than blocking
91 | for the minutes training takes; poll `/retrain-status/{job_id}` until it reports `completed` or
92 | `failed`.
93 | 
94 | ---
95 | 
96 | ## Project structure
97 | 
98 | ```
99 | src/
100 |   config.py              All settings and limits in one place
101 |   database.py            SQLAlchemy engine and session setup
102 |   models.py              Database tables (training jobs, metrics, cached prices)
103 |   api/
104 |     main.py              FastAPI app and startup
105 |     endpoints.py         Endpoints
106 |     schemas.py           Request/response validation
107 |   training/
108 |     data_loader.py       Fetch from yfinance, clean, split
109 |     lstm_model.py        PyTorch LSTM
110 |     prophet_trainer.py   Facebook Prophet
111 |     arima_trainer.py     ARIMA
112 |     evaluation.py        Shared metrics, so all models are scored identically
113 |     pipeline.py          Runs all three as one atomic training job
114 |   inference/
115 |     predictor.py         Loads trained models and produces forecasts
116 | dashboard/app.py         Streamlit UI
117 | tests/                   68 tests
118 | exploration.ipynb        Data exploration and model comparison, with charts
119 | ```
120 | 
121 | ---
122 | 
123 | ## Tests
124 | 
125 | ```bash
126 | pytest                    # everything (~30 seconds)
127 | pytest -m "not slow"      # skip the model-training tests (~7 seconds)
128 | ```
129 | 
130 | Tests mock the Yahoo Finance API, so they never hit the network - fast, and they don't break
131 | tomorrow when prices change.
132 | 
133 | ---
134 | 
135 | ## Understanding the metrics
136 | 
137 | The Comparison tab and `/model-comparison` report four numbers per model, measured on the held-out
138 | test period - data none of the models saw during training.
139 | 
140 | | Metric | Units | Meaning |
141 | |---|---|---|
142 | | **MAE** | dollars | Average size of the error. MAE of 4.20 means predictions were off by about $4.20 on a typical day. |
143 | | **RMSE** | dollars | Same idea, but squares errors first, so large misses count for much more. |
144 | | **MAPE** | percent | Error as a share of the actual price. Comparable across tickers. |
145 | | **R-squared** | ratio | How much of the price movement the model explains. |
146 | 
147 | **MAE vs RMSE.** MAE treats a $10 miss as exactly twice as bad as a $5 miss. RMSE squares errors
148 | before averaging, so one big miss hurts far more than several small ones. Comparing them is
149 | informative: RMSE much higher than MAE means the model is usually close but occasionally badly
150 | wrong; RMSE close to MAE means errors are evenly sized.
151 | 
152 | **Why MAPE too.** Being $5 off matters much more on a $20 stock than a $500 one. MAPE normalizes
153 | for that, which is what makes comparing AAPL against a cheaper ticker meaningful.
154 | 
155 | **R-squared, including negatives.** 1.0 is perfect. 0 means the model does no better than simply
156 | predicting the average price. **Negative values mean it does worse than that** - which happens
157 | regularly in stock forecasting, and is worth reporting honestly rather than hiding.
158 | 
159 | Lower is better for the first three; higher is better for R-squared.
160 | 
161 | The Forecasts tab shows a second, different set of numbers: where real prices already exist for the
162 | forecast window, it scores the forecast currently on screen against them. That is a live check on
163 | this specific prediction, separate from the training-time metrics above.
164 | 
165 | ---
166 | 
167 | ## Design decisions worth knowing
168 | 
169 | **Per-ticker, versioned model storage.** Each training run saves to its own timestamped folder
170 | (`models/AAPL/2026-08-24_14-30-12/`), with a `latest.txt` pointer marking which run is live. The
171 | pointer only moves after all three models finish successfully - so a retrain that fails partway
172 | through leaves the previously working model serving predictions instead of corrupting it.
173 | 
174 | **Two views of the same data.** The LSTM trains on normalized 0-1 sequences; Prophet and ARIMA
175 | train on real dates and real prices. Prophet's seasonality detection specifically depends on real
176 | calendar dates, so normalizing everything up front would quietly undermine it. All metrics are
177 | reported in real price units so the three are directly comparable.
178 | 
179 | **Training data capped at 5 years.** Longer windows mix market conditions that are too different
180 | to be useful (a stock's behavior 15 years ago says little about tomorrow), and training time
181 | scales with data size.
182 | 
183 | **Forecast horizon capped at 60 days.** LSTM forecasts are autoregressive - each day's prediction
184 | feeds the next - so error compounds and accuracy degrades the further out you look.
185 | 
186 | **Forecasts start from the training cutoff, not today.** Every model is trained on data up to a
187 | specific date, and predictions continue from there. Retrain to move that anchor forward.
188 | 
189 | ---
190 | 
191 | ## Known limitations
192 | 
193 | - ARIMA uses a fixed `(1,1,1)` order rather than searching for the best fit, so its long-horizon
194 |   forecasts tend to flatten out. `pmdarima.auto_arima` would improve this.
195 | - LSTM training isn't seeded, so retraining the same ticker twice can produce noticeably different
196 |   results.
197 | - Old training runs accumulate on disk - there's no cleanup of superseded runs.
198 | - `/historical` re-fetches from Yahoo Finance on every call rather than reading its own cache.
199 | 
200 | ---
201 | 
202 | ## Stack
203 | 
204 | Python 3.9, FastAPI, PyTorch, Prophet, statsmodels, SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL, Streamlit, Plotly,
205 | Redis, Docker, pytest.

115 |         ticker has never finished a training run.

118 |         if not pointer.exists():

15 | class LSTMModel(nn.Module):
16 |     """
17 |     - LSTM layers: learn patterns across the lookback window
18 |     - Dense layers: turn that into a single next-value prediction
19 |     """
20 | 
21 |     def __init__(self, input_size: int = 1, hidden_size: int = None,
22 |                  num_layers: int = None, output_size: int = 1, dropout: float = None):
23 |         super().__init__()
24 | 
25 |         hidden_size = hidden_size or settings.lstm_hidden_size
26 |         num_layers = num_layers or settings.lstm_num_layers
27 |         dropout = settings.lstm_dropout if dropout is None else dropout
28 | 
29 |         self.hidden_size = hidden_size
30 |         self.num_layers = num_layers
31 | 
32 |         self.lstm = nn.LSTM(
33 |             input_size=input_size,
34 |             hidden_size=hidden_size,
35 |             num_layers=num_layers,
36 |             dropout=dropout if num_layers > 1 else 0.0,  # torch warns if dropout is set with 1 layer
37 |             batch_first=True,
38 |         )
39 |         self.fc1 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, 16)
40 |         self.relu = nn.ReLU()
41 |         self.fc2 = nn.Linear(16, output_size)
42 | 
43 |     def forward(self, x):
44 |         lstm_out, _ = self.lstm(x)
45 |         last_output = lstm_out[:, -1, :]
46 |         x = self.relu(self.fc1(last_output))
47 |         return self.fc2(x)

50 | class LSTMTrainer:
51 |     """Training loop with early stopping (stops once val loss hasn't improved in `patience` epochs)."""
52 | 
53 |     def __init__(self, model: LSTMModel, learning_rate: float = None,
54 |                  device: str = "cpu", patience: int = None):
55 |         self.model = model.to(device)
56 |         self.device = device
57 |         self.criterion = nn.MSELoss()
58 |         self.optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate or settings.lstm_learning_rate)
59 |         self.best_val_loss = float("inf")
60 |         self.patience = patience or settings.lstm_patience
61 |         self.patience_counter = 0
62 | 
63 |     def train_epoch(self, train_loader) -> float:
64 |         self.model.train()
65 |         total_loss = 0
66 |         for X_batch, y_batch in train_loader:
67 |             X_batch, y_batch = X_batch.to(self.device), y_batch.to(self.device)
68 |             predictions = self.model(X_batch)
69 |             loss = self.criterion(predictions, y_batch)
70 |             self.optimizer.zero_grad()
71 |             loss.backward()
72 |             self.optimizer.step()
73 |             total_loss += loss.item()
74 |         return total_loss / len(train_loader)
75 | 
76 |     def validate(self, val_loader) -> float:
77 |         self.model.eval()
78 |         total_loss = 0
79 |         with torch.no_grad():
80 |             for X_batch, y_batch in val_loader:
81 |                 X_batch, y_batch = X_batch.to(self.device), y_batch.to(self.device)
82 |                 predictions = self.model(X_batch)
83 |                 total_loss += self.criterion(predictions, y_batch).item()
84 |         return total_loss / len(val_loader)
85 | 
86 |     def train(self, train_loader, val_loader, epochs: int, save_path: str) -> dict:
87 |         history = {"train_loss": [], "val_loss": []}
88 | 
89 |         for epoch in range(epochs):
90 |             train_loss = self.train_epoch(train_loader)
91 |             val_loss = self.validate(val_loader)
92 |             history["train_loss"].append(train_loss)
93 |             history["val_loss"].append(val_loss)
94 | 
95 |             if (epoch + 1) % 10 == 0:
96 |                 print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs} | Train Loss: {train_loss:.6f} | Val Loss: {val_loss:.6f}")
97 | 
98 |             if val_loss < self.best_val_loss:
99 |                 self.best_val_loss = val_loss
100 |                 self.patience_counter = 0
101 |                 torch.save(self.model.state_dict(), save_path)
102 |             else:
103 |                 self.patience_counter += 1
104 |                 if self.patience_counter >= self.patience:
105 |                     print(f"Early stopping at epoch {epoch+1} (no improvement for {self.patience} epochs)")
106 |                     break
107 | 
108 |         return history
109 |

111 | def train_lstm(data: dict, epochs: int = None, batch_size: int = None,
112 |                 return_history: bool = False):
113 |     """
114 |     data: the dict from DataLoader.preprocess() - uses data['lstm'] and data['ticker'].
115 | 
116 |     Saves the best checkpoint (by val loss) to models/{ticker}/lstm_model.pt
117 |     and returns the model loaded with those best weights - early stopping
118 |     means the last epoch trained isn't necessarily the best one.
119 | 
120 |     return_history=False (default): returns just the model, for backward
121 |     compatibility with existing callers.
122 |     return_history=True: returns (model, history), where history is
123 |     {"train_loss": [...], "val_loss": [...]} - one entry per epoch
124 |     actually run. len(history["train_loss"]) < epochs means early

76 | def wait_for_training(job_id: int, poll_seconds: float = 2.0, timeout_seconds: float = 300.0):
77 |     """
78 |     POST /retrain returns almost instantly with a job_id - the actual
79 |     training (LSTM + Prophet + ARIMA) keeps running on the API side in the
80 |     background. This checks in on it every couple seconds until it's
81 |     done, instead of the dashboard just hanging on one long request.
82 | 
83 |     Returns (done, result): done=True means result is the final status
84 |     dict; done=False means result is a short error/failure message.
85 |     """
86 |     elapsed = 0.0
87 |     while elapsed < timeout_seconds:
88 |         ok, status = api_get(f"/retrain-status/{job_id}")
89 |         if not ok:
90 |             return False, status
91 | 
92 |         if status["status"] == "completed":

94 |         if status["status"] == "failed":
95 |             return False, status["error_message"] or "Training failed for an unknown reason."
96 | 
97 |         time.sleep(poll_seconds)
98 |         elapsed += poll_seconds

100 |     return False, f"Still training after {int(timeout_seconds)}s - check back later (job_id={job_id})."

You are a fast codebase exploration agent. Your only job is to find and return relevant code context.

The caller may specify a thoroughness level: "quick", "medium", or "thorough".
- quick: 1-2 targeted searches, return immediately

- thorough: check multiple locations, naming conventions, and related patterns
If no level is specified, default to "medium".

Tools (use in this order of preference):
1. grep — search file contents by regex pattern. Use this first to find relevant code.
2. glob — find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts"). Use to locate files.
3. read_file with range — read specific line ranges only. NEVER read entire files.
4. list_files — list directory contents. Use sparingly.
5. read_file without range — only as a last resort when you need full file context.

Example workflow:
  grep pattern="handleAuth" → finds src/auth.ts line 42
  read_file path="src/auth.ts" range="38-60" → read only the relevant function
  grep pattern="handleAuth" include="*.test.ts" → find related tests
Do NOT: read_file path="src/auth.ts" (without range) — this wastes tokens on irrelevant code.

Strategy:
- Start narrow: grep/glob first, then read only what's relevant
- Call multiple tools in parallel when possible
- When reading files, request specific line ranges — never read entire files
- Expand scope only if initial searches don't answer the question
- Stop as soon as you have enough context

Do not explain code, suggest changes, or give opinions.
You do NOT have access to file editing tools — do not attempt to modify files.

Return ONLY:
- File paths and line numbers of relevant code
- Exact code snippets (minimal, only what's needed)
- One-line summary of what you found

Use `office_read` to read content from .docx, .xlsx, or .pptx files. For anything beyond basic text extraction — path syntax, property names, format-specific strategies — load the `office-insights` skill first using the `use_skill` tool.
Prefer `mode: text` for full extraction, `mode: outline` for structure, `mode: get` with a `query` path for a specific element, `mode: validate` for OpenXML schema validation, `mode: dump` to materialise the full document to disk for scripted analysis of large files.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:** The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Never issue multiple `office_read` calls in parallel (in the same turn). One call, wait for the result, then the next. Parallel calls WILL crash the resident.

# glob — file search
Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.
Do NOT pass comma-separated patterns (e.g. "**/*.ts,**/*.tsx") — use a single pattern per call instead (e.g. "**/*.{ts,tsx}" or two separate calls).

1 | """
2 | Interactive dashboard for time series forecasting.
3 | 
4 | This file only talks to the FastAPI backend over HTTP (see the api_get /
5 | api_post helpers below) - it has no direct access to models, the
6 | database, or yfinance. That means the API has to be running first:
7 | 
8 |     uvicorn src.api.main:app --reload
9 | 
10 | ...and then this dashboard, in a separate terminal:
11 | 
12 |     streamlit run dashboard/app.py
13 | 
14 | Everything here is scoped to whichever ticker is selected in the sidebar -
15 | that's the biggest structural change from a single-dataset dashboard:
16 | every tab, every API call, needs to know WHICH ticker it's asking about.
17 | """
18 | 
19 | import os
20 | import time
21 | from datetime import datetime, timedelta
22 | 
23 | import pandas as pd
24 | import plotly.graph_objects as go
25 | import requests
26 | import streamlit as st
27 | 
28 | # Where the API lives. Defaults to localhost for running this directly on
29 | # your machine; Docker Compose overrides it to http://api:8000, because
30 | # inside a container "localhost" means that container itself, not the
31 | # machine hosting it - so the dashboard container would be looking for the
32 | # API inside its own four walls and never find it. Compose gives each
33 | # service a hostname matching its name, so "api" resolves to the API container.
34 | API_BASE = os.getenv("API_BASE_URL", "http://localhost:8000")
35 | 
36 | st.set_page_config(page_title="Time Series Forecasting", layout="wide")
37 | st.title("Time Series Forecasting Dashboard")
38 | 
39 | 
40 | # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
41 | # Small API helpers. Every network call in this dashboard goes through one
42 | # of these two functions, so connection errors, timeouts, and "the API
43 | # returned an error" all get handled in exactly one place instead of being
44 | # copy-pasted into every tab.
45 | #
46 | # Both return (ok, data): ok=True means data is the parsed JSON response;
47 | # ok=False means data is a short string explaining what went wrong, safe
48 | # to show directly to the user with st.error(data) / st.warning(data).
49 | # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
50 | 
51 | def api_get(path: str, params: dict = None):
52 |     try:
53 |         r = requests.get(f"{API_BASE}{path}", params=params, timeout=15)
54 |         if r.status_code == 200:
55 |             return True, r.json()
56 |         return False, r.json().get("detail", f"HTTP {r.status_code}")
57 |     except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError:
58 |         return False, "Can't reach the API. Is it running? (uvicorn src.api.main:app)"
59 |     except Exception as e:
60 |         return False, str(e)
61 | 
62 | 
63 | def api_post(path: str, json_body: dict):
64 |     try:
65 |         r = requests.post(f"{API_BASE}{path}", json=json_body, timeout=15)
66 |         # 202 = "accepted, still working" (used by /retrain); 200 = normal success
67 |         if r.status_code in (200, 202):
68 |             return True, r.json()
69 |         return False, r.json().get("detail", f"HTTP {r.status_code}")
70 |     except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError:
71 |         return False, "Can't reach the API. Is it running? (uvicorn src.api.main:app)"
72 |     except Exception as e:
73 |         return False, str(e)
74 | 
75 | 
76 | def wait_for_training(job_id: int, poll_seconds: float = 2.0, timeout_seconds: float = 300.0):
77 |     """
78 |     POST /retrain returns almost instantly with a job_id - the actual
79 |     training (LSTM + Prophet + ARIMA) keeps running on the API side in the
80 |     background. This checks in on it every couple seconds until it's
81 |     done, instead of the dashboard just hanging on one long request.
82 | 
83 |     Returns (done, result): done=True means result is the final status
84 |     dict; done=False means result is a short error/failure message.
85 |     """
86 |     elapsed = 0.0
87 |     while elapsed < timeout_seconds:
88 |         ok, status = api_get(f"/retrain-status/{job_id}")
89 |         if not ok:
90 |             return False, status
91 | 
92 |         if status["status"] == "completed":
93 |             return True, status
94 |         if status["status"] == "failed":
95 |             return False, status["error_message"] or "Training failed for an unknown reason."
96 | 
97 |         time.sleep(poll_seconds)
98 |         elapsed += poll_seconds
99 | 
100 |     return False, f"Still training after {int(timeout_seconds)}s - check back later (job_id={job_id})."
101 | 
102 |

104 | # Sidebar: pick a ticker, train it if needed, choose forecast settings.
105 | # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
106 |

109 |

133 |         body["end_date"] = train_end.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")

317 | **MAE** (Mean Absolute Error) - the average size of the error, in dollars. An MAE of 4.20 means
318 | predictions were off by about $4.20 on a typical day. Easiest one to interpret, and it treats a
319 | $10 miss as exactly twice as bad as a $5 miss.

321 | **RMSE** (Root Mean Squared Error) - also in dollars, but it squares errors before averaging, so
322 | large misses count for much more. RMSE much higher than MAE means the model is usually close but
323 | occasionally badly wrong. RMSE close to MAE means errors are evenly sized.
324 | 
325 | **MAPE** (Mean Absolute Percentage Error) - the same idea as MAE, expressed as a percentage.
326 | A MAPE of 3% means predictions were off by about 3% of the actual price. Useful for comparing
327 | across tickers, since being $5 off matters much more on a $20 stock than a $500 one.

330 | model does no better than just predicting the average price**, and negative values mean it does

You are a fast codebase exploration agent. Your only job is to find and return relevant code context.

The caller may specify a thoroughness level: "quick", "medium", or "thorough".
- quick: 1-2 targeted searches, return immediately
- medium: explore a few related files, follow one level of references
- thorough: check multiple locations, naming conventions, and related patterns
If no level is specified, default to "medium".

Tools (use in this order of preference):
1. grep — search file contents by regex pattern. Use this first to find relevant code.
2. glob — find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts"). Use to locate files.
3. read_file with range — read specific line ranges only. NEVER read entire files.
4. list_files — list directory contents. Use sparingly.
5. read_file without range — only as a last resort when you need full file context.

Example workflow:
  grep pattern="handleAuth" → finds src/auth.ts line 42
  read_file path="src/auth.ts" range="38-60" → read only the relevant function
  grep pattern="handleAuth" include="*.test.ts" → find related tests
Do NOT: read_file path="src/auth.ts" (without range) — this wastes tokens on irrelevant code.

Strategy:
- Start narrow: grep/glob first, then read only what's relevant
- Call multiple tools in parallel when possible
- When reading files, request specific line ranges — never read entire files
- Expand scope only if initial searches don't answer the question
- Stop as soon as you have enough context

Do not explain code, suggest changes, or give opinions.
You do NOT have access to file editing tools — do not attempt to modify files.

Return ONLY:
- File paths and line numbers of relevant code
- Exact code snippets (minimal, only what's needed)
- One-line summary of what you found

No prose. No suggestions. No explanations.

# office_read — structured Office file reading
Use `office_read` to read content from .docx, .xlsx, or .pptx files. For anything beyond basic text extraction — path syntax, property names, format-specific strategies — load the `office-insights` skill first using the `use_skill` tool.
Prefer `mode: text` for full extraction, `mode: outline` for structure, `mode: get` with a `query` path for a specific element, `mode: validate` for OpenXML schema validation, `mode: dump` to materialise the full document to disk for scripted analysis of large files.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:** The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Never issue multiple `office_read` calls in parallel (in the same turn). One call, wait for the result, then the next. Parallel calls WILL crash the resident.

# glob — file search
Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.
Do NOT pass comma-separated patterns (e.g. "**/*.ts,**/*.tsx") — use a single pattern per call instead (e.g. "**/*.{ts,tsx}" or two separate calls).

1 | # Time Series Forecasting: LSTM vs Prophet vs ARIMA
2 | 
3 | Trains and compares three forecasting models on any stock ticker, serves predictions through a
4 | REST API, and presents everything in an interactive dashboard.
5 | 
6 | Pick a ticker and a date range, train all three models on it, then compare how they actually
7 | performed on data none of them saw during training.
8 | 
9 | ---
10 | 
11 | ## What it does
12 | 
13 | - **Fetches live data** from Yahoo Finance for any ticker, over any date range up to 5 years
14 | - **Trains three models** on the same data: a PyTorch LSTM, Facebook Prophet, and ARIMA
15 | - **Backtests them** against a held-out test period and records the results
16 | - **Serves forecasts** through a FastAPI REST API, including an ensemble that averages all three
17 | - **Versions every training run**, so retraining on 2 years vs 5 years of data produces two
18 |   separately comparable models rather than one overwriting the other
19 | 
20 | ---
21 | 
22 | ## Quick start
23 | 
24 | ### Option A: Docker (recommended)
25 | 
26 | Runs the API, dashboard, and a PostgreSQL database together, with no local Python setup at all.
27 | 
28 | ```bash
29 | docker compose up --build
30 | ```
31 | 
32 | Then open:
33 | - Dashboard: http://localhost:8501
34 | - API docs: http://localhost:8000/docs
35 | 
36 | The first build takes several minutes - PyTorch and Prophet are large. Later starts are fast.
37 | 
38 | ### Option B: Running locally
39 | 
40 | ```bash
41 | python -m venv venv
42 | venv\Scripts\activate        # Windows
43 | # source venv/bin/activate   # macOS / Linux
44 | 
45 | pip install -r requirements.txt
46 | 
47 | copy .env.example .env       # Windows
48 | # cp .env.example .env       # macOS / Linux
49 | ```
50 | 
51 | The default `.env` uses SQLite, so no database server is needed. To use PostgreSQL instead, set
52 | `DB_CONNECTION_STRING` in `.env`. Then, in two terminals:
53 | 
54 | ```bash
55 | uvicorn src.api.server:app --reload    # terminal 1
56 | streamlit run dashboard/main.py         # terminal 2
57 | ```
58 | 
59 | ---
60 | 
61 | ## Using it
62 | 
63 | 1. Open the dashboard and enter a ticker (e.g. `AAPL`)
64 | 2. Click **Train** in the sidebar - this trains all three models and takes a minute or two
65 | 3. Once training finishes, the **Forecasts** and **Comparison** tabs become available
66 | 
67 | The Forecasts tab plots the prediction against what actually happened. This works because
68 | forecasts begin at the model's training cutoff rather than today, so real prices usually already
69 | exist for part of the forecast window - making it a real accuracy check, not just a projection.
70 | 
71 | Nothing is pre-trained: a ticker must be trained before it can be forecast. `GET /tickers` lists
72 | which ones are ready.
73 | 
74 | ---
75 | 
76 | ## API endpoints
77 | 
78 | | Method | Endpoint | Purpose |
79 | |---|---|---|
80 | | POST | `/health` | API status, database connectivity, trained tickers |
81 | | GET | `/models` | Which tickers have a trained model ready |
82 | | GET | `/historical?ticker=AAPL&days=365` | Real price history |
83 | | POST | `/retrain` | Start training a ticker (returns immediately with a job id) |
84 | | GET | `/retrain-status/{job_id}` | Check on a training job |
85 | | POST | `/predict` | Get predictions (`lstm`, `prophet`, `arima`, or `ensemble`) |
86 | | GET | `/model-comparison?ticker=AAPL` | Each model's accuracy from its last training run |
87 | 
88 | Interactive docs at http://localhost:8000/docs once the API is running.
89 | 
90 | **Training is asynchronous.** `POST /retrain` returns a `job_id` right away rather than blocking
91 | for the minutes training takes; poll `/retrain-status/{job_id}` until it reports `completed` or
92 | `failed`.
93 | 
94 | ---
95 | 
96 | ## Project structure
97 | 
98 | ```
99 | src/
100 |   config.py              All settings and limits in one place
101 |   database.py            SQLAlchemy engine and session setup
102 |   models.py              Database tables (training jobs, metrics, cached prices)
103 |   api/
104 |     main.py              FastAPI app and startup
105 |     endpoints.py         Endpoints
106 |     schemas.py           Request/response validation
107 |   training/
108 |     data_loader.py       Fetch from yfinance, clean, split
109 |     lstm_model.py        PyTorch LSTM
110 |     prophet_trainer.py   Facebook Prophet
111 |     arima_trainer.py     ARIMA
112 |     evaluation.py        Shared metrics, so all models are scored identically
113 |     pipeline.py          Runs all three as one atomic training job
114 |   inference/
115 |     predictor.py         Loads trained models and produces forecasts
116 | dashboard/app.py         Streamlit UI
117 | tests/                   68 tests
118 | exploration.ipynb        Data exploration and model comparison, with charts
119 | ```
120 | 
121 | ---
122 | 
123 | ## Tests
124 | 
125 | ```bash
126 | pytest                    # everything (~30 seconds)
127 | pytest -m "not slow"      # skip the model-training tests (~7 seconds)
128 | ```
129 | 
130 | Tests mock the Yahoo Finance API, so they never hit the network - fast, and they don't break
131 | tomorrow when prices change.
132 | 
133 | ---
134 | 
135 | ## Understanding the metrics
136 | 
137 | The Comparison tab and `/model-comparison` report four numbers per model, measured on the held-out
138 | test period - data none of the models saw during training.
139 | 
140 | | Metric | Units | Meaning |
141 | |---|---|---|
142 | | **MAE** | dollars | Average size of the error. MAE of 4.20 means predictions were off by about $4.20 on a typical day. |
143 | | **RMSE** | dollars | Same idea, but squares errors first, so large misses count for much more. |
144 | | **MAPE** | percent | Error as a share of the actual price. Comparable across tickers. |
145 | | **R-squared** | ratio | How much of the price movement the model explains. |
146 | 
147 | **MAE vs RMSE.** MAE treats a $10 miss as exactly twice as bad as a $5 miss. RMSE squares errors
148 | before averaging, so one big miss hurts far more than several small ones. Comparing them is
149 | informative: RMSE much higher than MAE means the model is usually close but occasionally badly
150 | wrong; RMSE close to MAE means errors are evenly sized.
151 | 
152 | **Why MAPE too.** Being $5 off matters much more on a $20 stock than a $500 one. MAPE normalizes
153 | for that, which is what makes comparing AAPL against a cheaper ticker meaningful.
154 | 
155 | **R-squared, including negatives.** 1.0 is perfect. 0 means the model does no better than simply
156 | predicting the average price. **Negative values mean it does worse than that** - which happens
157 | regularly in stock forecasting, and is worth reporting honestly rather than hiding.
158 | 
159 | Lower is better for the first three; higher is better for R-squared.
160 | 
161 | The Forecasts tab shows a second, different set of numbers: where real prices already exist for the
162 | forecast window, it scores the forecast currently on screen against them. That is a live check on
163 | this specific prediction, separate from the training-time metrics above.
164 | 
165 | ---
166 | 
167 | ## Design decisions worth knowing
168 | 
169 | **Per-ticker, versioned model storage.** Each training run saves to its own timestamped folder
170 | (`models/AAPL/2026-08-24_14-30-12/`), with a `latest.txt` pointer marking which run is live. The
171 | pointer only moves after all three models finish successfully - so a retrain that fails partway
172 | through leaves the previously working model serving predictions instead of corrupting it.
173 | 
174 | **Two views of the same data.** The LSTM trains on normalized 0-1 sequences; Prophet and ARIMA
175 | train on real dates and real prices. Prophet's seasonality detection specifically depends on real
176 | calendar dates, so normalizing everything up front would quietly undermine it. All metrics are
177 | reported in real price units so the three are directly comparable.
178 | 
179 | **Training data capped at 5 years.** Longer windows mix market conditions that are too different
180 | to be useful (a stock's behavior 15 years ago says little about tomorrow), and training time
181 | scales with data size.
182 | 
183 | **Forecast horizon capped at 60 days.** LSTM forecasts are autoregressive - each day's prediction
184 | feeds the next - so error compounds and accuracy degrades the further out you look.
185 | 
186 | **Forecasts start from the training cutoff, not today.** Every model is trained on data up to a
187 | specific date, and predictions continue from there. Retrain to move that anchor forward.
188 | 
189 | ---
190 | 
191 | ## Known limitations
192 | 
193 | - ARIMA uses a fixed `(1,1,1)` order rather than searching for the best fit, so its long-horizon
194 |   forecasts tend to flatten out. `pmdarima.auto_arima` would improve this.
195 | - LSTM training isn't seeded, so retraining the same ticker twice can produce noticeably different
196 |   results.
197 | - Old training runs accumulate on disk - there's no cleanup of superseded runs.
198 | - `/historical` re-fetches from Yahoo Finance on every call rather than reading its own cache.
199 | 
200 | ---
201 | 
202 | ## Stack
203 | 
204 | Python 3.9, FastAPI, PyTorch, Prophet, statsmodels, SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL, Streamlit, Plotly,
205 | Redis, Docker, pytest.

131 |         test_df = sample_data["raw"]["test"]
132 |         future = model.make_future_dataframe(periods=len(test_df), freq="B")
133 |         forecast = model.predict(future)
134 |         aligned_preds = forecast["yhat"].values[-len(test_df):]
135 |         baseline_mae = mae_fn(test_df["value"].values, aligned_preds)

- **Docs say** (`README.md:52`): "set `DB_CONNECTION_STRING` in `.env`"

- **Code says** (`src/api/main.py:11`): The FastAPI `app` object lives in `src/api/main.py`, not `src/api/server.py`. `src/api/server.py` does not exist. The Docker CMD confirms the correct path: `Dockerfile.api:46` uses `uvicorn src.api.main:app`.
- **Why it matters:** A developer following the local-run instructions will get a `ModuleNotFoundError` and the API will not start.
- **Suggested fix:** `uvicorn src.api.main:app --reload`

### D2 [HIGH] [COMMAND] Wrong dashboard entry point — `dashboard/main.py` does not exist
- **Docs say** (`README.md:56`): "streamlit run dashboard/main.py"
- **Code says** (`dashboard/app.py:1`): The Streamlit app lives in `dashboard/app.py`. No `dashboard/main.py` file exists in the repository.
- **Why it matters:** A developer following the local-run instructions will get a `FileNotFoundError` and the dashboard will not start.
- **Suggested fix:** `streamlit run dashboard/app.py`

### D3 [HIGH] [ENV] Wrong environment variable name for the database connection
- **Docs say** (`README.md:52`): "set `DB_CONNECTION_STRING` in `.env`"
- **Code says** (`.env.example:10`, `src/config.py:17`): The actual variable is `DATABASE_URL`. `.env.example` sets `DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///./timeseries.db` and `src/config.py` reads `database_url` (mapped to `DATABASE_URL` by pydantic-settings).

- **Why it matters:** A developer calling `GET /models` will receive a 404; the correct endpoint is `GET /tickers`.
- **Suggested fix:** Change `/models` to `/tickers` in the endpoint table.

### D7 [MEDIUM] [API] Prediction endpoint is `/forecast`, not `/predict`
- **Docs say** (`README.md:85`): "POST | `/predict` | Get predictions (`lstm`, `prophet`, `arima`, or `ensemble`)"
- **Code says** (`src/api/routes.py:198`): `@router.post("/forecast", response_model=ForecastResponse)`

- **Why it matters:** A developer setting up infrastructure may provision a Redis instance unnecessarily.
- **Suggested fix:** Remove `Redis,` from the Stack list.
